title: Ridgeline Electric — rocky start, discovery rescue
description: Rep (Maya, Relay) starts by pitching Priya, GM of a 14-electrician contractor, who pushes back hard on price and mentions they are fine with their current tool. The probability dips. Then the rep stops pitching, asks real discovery questions, quantifies the pain, and reframes the price against it. Priya re-engages, the decision process surfaces, and the call ends with an agreed pilot.

utterances.speaker: rep
utterances.text: Hi Priya, Maya from Relay. Thanks for the time today.

utterances.speaker: prospect
utterances.text: Hi Maya. I'll be honest, I only took this because our office manager kept forwarding your emails. We have a system already.

utterances.speaker: rep
utterances.text: Fair enough, I appreciate you being upfront. Let me give you the quick version of Relay then. It's a dispatch and scheduling platform for electrical contractors: automatic daily board, real-time re-dispatch, tech mobile app with job forms, customer SMS updates, and reporting on utilization and first-time fix. It plugs into your accounting so invoices flow through automatically.

utterances.speaker: prospect
utterances.text: That sounds like what we have. What does it cost?

utterances.speaker: rep
utterances.text: For fourteen electricians it's around nine hundred a month on the annual plan.

utterances.speaker: prospect
utterances.text: Nine hundred? We pay three fifty for what we've got. I'm not going to nearly triple our software cost for a nicer-looking calendar. That's a hard no from a budget standpoint.

utterances.speaker: rep
utterances.text: I understand. Relay does a lot more than a calendar though, the real-time re-dispatch alone is something most tools in that price range don't do, and the SMS updates dramatically cut inbound calls.

utterances.speaker: prospect
utterances.text: Maybe. Our tool is fine. The guys are used to it.

utterances.speaker: rep
utterances.text: Okay. Can I take a step back? I've been talking about Relay and I don't actually know anything about how your days go. What does a bad day look like for your dispatcher right now?

utterances.speaker: prospect
utterances.text: A bad day. Hm. A bad day is when a commercial job runs over and we've got three residential calls stacked behind it. Neha, our coordinator, has to call every one of them, and half the time she can't reach anyone, so a tech shows up to an empty house.

utterances.speaker: rep
utterances.text: How often does that happen, a tech arriving to an empty house or a cancelled job they didn't know about?

utterances.speaker: prospect
utterances.text: More than I'd like. Probably two or three times a week across the team. Each one is a wasted hour plus drive time.

utterances.speaker: rep
utterances.text: So call it ten to twelve wasted tech-hours a week. What does a loaded electrician hour cost you, roughly?

utterances.speaker: prospect
utterances.text: With the truck, about eighty-five dollars. So, what, a thousand a week? I hadn't done that math.

utterances.speaker: rep
utterances.text: About four thousand a month in wasted hours, before counting the customers who get annoyed. Does your current tool re-sequence the day automatically when a job runs over, or does Neha do that by hand?

utterances.speaker: prospect
utterances.text: By hand. It's a scheduling grid, it doesn't know a job is running over until she updates it. Which she can't do while she's on the phone.

utterances.speaker: rep
utterances.text: That's the gap I'd want to look at with you. What else is on Neha's plate that suffers when she's stuck on those calls?

utterances.speaker: prospect
utterances.text: Quoting. She's supposed to send quotes the same day and they slip to two or three days. We lose some of those to whoever quotes first.

utterances.speaker: rep
utterances.text: So there's slipped revenue on quotes too. Roughly how many quotes a month go out late?

utterances.speaker: prospect
utterances.text: Maybe fifteen. We win about a third of quotes normally, less when we're late. Average job is twelve hundred.

utterances.speaker: rep
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not going to pretend I can attribute all of that to scheduling. But if even two extra quotes a month land because Neha isn't on the phone re-shuffling, that's more than the difference between your current tool and Relay. Is that a fair way to look at it?

utterances.speaker: prospect
utterances.text: That's a fairer way to look at it than tripling my software bill, yes. Okay. I'm listening.

utterances.speaker: rep
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me be specific about the one thing that matters here rather than the whole feature list: when a job runs over, Relay re-sequences the remaining jobs for that tech, texts each customer a new window, and only flags Neha if someone replies that the new time doesn't work. Neha goes from making eight calls to handling one exception.

utterances.speaker: prospect
utterances.text: That would genuinely change her day. Does it work for commercial jobs where the contact is a site foreman rather than a homeowner?

utterances.speaker: rep
utterances.text: Yes, the contact per job can be anyone, and commercial jobs can be set to notify without offering a reschedule. How do you split commercial versus residential today?

utterances.speaker: prospect
utterances.text: About sixty-forty commercial. The commercial guys would want the foreman to get the text, not the office. Okay, that works.

utterances.speaker: rep
utterances.text: Good. Can I ask how a decision like this would get made at Ridgeline? Is it yours, or are there others involved?

utterances.speaker: prospect
utterances.text: It's mine up to about five hundred a month. Above that I'd bring it to Raj, he's the owner, but he generally goes with my recommendation on operations stuff.

utterances.speaker: rep
utterances.text: Understood. And is there a timeline you're working to, or is this more of a when-it-makes-sense thing?

utterances.speaker: prospect
utterances.text: Our current contract renews in August, so if we're going to switch, it needs to be decided by July. I don't want to pay for two tools.

utterances.speaker: rep
utterances.text: That makes sense, and it gives us time to do this properly. What would you and Raj need to see to be confident this isn't just a nicer calendar?

utterances.speaker: prospect
utterances.text: I'd want to see it handle a real week of our jobs. Not a demo with fake data. And I'd want Neha's opinion, she's the one living in it.

utterances.speaker: rep
utterances.text: Then let's do exactly that. We run a two-week pilot on your real job list, with Neha driving it and me on call. It's four hundred for the two weeks, credited against the first year if you go ahead, refunded if Neha says it's not better. Would that work for you?

utterances.speaker: prospect
utterances.text: That's reasonable. Four hundred is within my authority, so I don't even need Raj for the pilot. When could we start?

utterances.speaker: rep
utterances.text: I could have Neha set up next week. How about a forty-five minute kickoff with you and Neha on Monday or Tuesday, and then she runs her normal week in Relay?

utterances.speaker: prospect
utterances.text: Tuesday afternoon is better, Mondays are chaos. Two o'clock?

utterances.speaker: rep
utterances.text: Tuesday at two. I'll send the pilot agreement and a short one-pager with the numbers we worked out, the wasted hours and the quote timing, so you have it for Raj later.

utterances.speaker: prospect
utterances.text: Please do. Put the math in there, that's what he'll care about.

utterances.speaker: rep
utterances.text: Will do. One last thing: is there anything about the current tool you'd miss? I'd rather know now than find out in week two.

utterances.speaker: prospect
utterances.text: The invoice sync is the one thing that works well. If that breaks, Neha will hate you.

utterances.speaker: rep
utterances.text: Noted, we'll set up the accounting sync on day one of the pilot so she can compare. Thanks Priya, I appreciate you letting me start over.

utterances.speaker: prospect
utterances.text: Well, the second half was a much better call than the first. See you Tuesday.
